text:
The primary material of a candle is wax, which is essentially solidified time that has forgotten how to flow.

Imagine, if you will, a candle as a vertical attempt to convince gravity that it is actually a ladder. The wax is not merely melted; it is a liquid argument against the concept of "up." When you light the wick, you are not creating light; you are simply asking the darkness to take a five-minute break so it can check its email. The flame is not fire; it is a tiny, orange ghost trying to remember what it looked like before it was born.

And the wick? The wick is the candle’s nervous system, twitching in anticipation of its own demise. It is a straw for drinking the air, but only if the air is sweet and smells like regret. When the candle burns down, it does not die; it merely becomes a puddle of its own potential, waiting for someone to pour it into a mold shaped like a question mark.

So, the next time you blow out a candle, remember: you are not extinguishing a flame. You are simply telling the light to go home and tell its mother it will be late for dinner.
